title: Ensure the default administrator password has been changed
description: Multifunction printers ship with blank or published default admin credentials (often printed in the manual or derived from the serial number). Default credentials give full control of network settings, stored jobs, address books and firmware.
reference: CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 - Change default administrator password (verify section number for your release)

audit.command: In the Embedded Web Server (EWS: browse to https://<printer-ip>/ and sign in as administrator; HP: Security / Networking tabs, Xerox: Properties > Security / Connectivity, Ricoh: Device Management > Configuration, Canon: Settings/Registration > Network Settings / Security Settings): confirm an administrator password is set and differs from the vendor default (try the documented default, e.g. blank, 'admin', '1111', 'x-admin' or the serial number, and expect it to be rejected). Also check the control-panel/service PIN and the SNMP write community. Confirm the password is unique per device and stored in the password vault; prefer LDAP/Kerberos-backed admin accounts where supported.

remediation.command: EWS: Security > General Security / Account management > set a unique, strong (15+ chars) administrator password; change the device service/control-panel PIN; restrict admin sign-in to directory-backed accounts where supported. Fleet: push via the vendor fleet tool (HP Web Jetadmin / Security Manager, Xerox CentreWare, Ricoh Streamline NX).

title: Limit Physical Access to Device
description: It is recommended that physical access to the MFD be restricted to only authorized users. Additionally, consider segregating print use by data classification or label. For example, it may be inappropriate for personnel from shipping to access a MFD used by the human resources department. Restricting physical access to the MFD will limit threats against the device’s hardware and protect the confidentiality of print, scan, and fax data.
reference: CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 - 1.1.1 Limit Physical Access to Device

audit.command: Verify compliance with CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 section 1.1.1: Limit Physical Access to Device.

remediation.command: Follow the remediation procedure in CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 section 1.1.1 to configure: Limit Physical Access to Device.

title: Configure Hard Drive Encryption
description: MFDs often support the ability to encrypt print jobs while at rest on internal hard drives. Enabling drive encryption will help ensure the confidentiality of sensitive data in the event a hard disk is stolen or discarded in an insecure manner.
reference: CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 - 1.2.1 Configure Hard Drive Encryption

audit.command: Verify compliance with CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 section 1.2.1: Configure Hard Drive Encryption.

remediation.command: Follow the remediation procedure in CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 section 1.2.1 to configure: Configure Hard Drive Encryption.

title: Set Static DNS Server Addresses
description: The Domain Name System (DNS) is a naming system for networked computers, devices, and resources. It is typically leveraged by network participants to resolve names to and from IP addresses. Network devices commonly support the ability to obtain DNS server addresses via two distinct methods; statically and dynamically. Statically assigned DNS server addresses are typically stored within the device’s NVRAM. Dynamically assigned DNS addresses are typically obtained at device boot-time via one of many network-based broadcast mechanisms. It is recommended that DNS server IP addresses be statically configured in the MFD. The use of static DNS server addresses reduces the device’s exposure to attacks against broadcast IP configuration mechanisms, such as DHCP and BOOTP. DHCP and other broadcast mechanisms utilize a UDP transport, which is susceptible to spoofing. If a malicious entity is abl...
reference: CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 - 2.1.2 Set Static DNS Server Addresses

audit.command: Verify compliance with CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 section 2.1.2: Set Static DNS Server Addresses.

remediation.command: Follow the remediation procedure in CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 section 2.1.2 to configure: Set Static DNS Server Addresses.

title: Require Valid and Trusted Signature for all Applications
description: Many enterprise class MFDs have development platforms that allow corporations to load software packages onto the device. These packages are typically designed to alter user interfaces, perform pre or post job processing such as encryption, or perform network operations. MFDs having this capability may support a configuration that requires all packages contain a valid digital signature of a trusted application developer. Ensuring the integrity and authenticity of applications and software packages installed on the MFD will ensure print job confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Configuring the MFD to require all packages and application contain a valid digital signature of a trusted developer will assist in this assurance.
reference: CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.1 Require Valid and Trusted Signature for all Applications

audit.command: Verify compliance with CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 section 4.1.1: Require Valid and Trusted Signature for all Applications.

remediation.command: Follow the remediation procedure in CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 section 4.1.1 to configure: Require Valid and Trusted Signature for all Applications.

title: Require Application Certificate be signed by a Trusted Authority
description: Many enterprise class MFDs allow corporations to load software packages onto the device. These packages are typically designed alter user interfaces, perform pre or post job processing such as encryption, or perform network operations. MFDs having this capability may support a configuration that requires all packages contain a certificate that has been signed by a trusted certificate authority (CA), or root. Ensuring that all application certificates are signed by a trusted root will ensure the authenticity of the application’s signature. This will in turn provide additional assurance that the integrity of the application being loaded on to the MFD is intact.
reference: CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.2 Require Application Certificate be signed by a Trusted Authority

audit.command: Verify compliance with CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 section 4.1.2: Require Application Certificate be signed by a Trusted Authority.

remediation.command: Follow the remediation procedure in CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 section 4.1.2 to configure: Require Application Certificate be signed by a Trusted Authority.

title: Ensure printer firmware is current and only signed firmware can be installed
description: Printer firmware regularly receives fixes for remotely exploitable flaws (PJL/PostScript, IPP, EWS). Accepting unsigned firmware allows persistent implants.
reference: CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 - Firmware updates / firmware integrity (verify section number for your release)

audit.command: In the Embedded Web Server (EWS: browse to https://<printer-ip>/ and sign in as administrator; HP: Security / Networking tabs, Xerox: Properties > Security / Connectivity, Ricoh: Device Management > Configuration, Canon: Settings/Registration > Network Settings / Security Settings): read the firmware version (HP: Information > Configuration Page / Firmware Upgrade; Xerox: Properties > General Setup > Configuration Report) and compare it with the latest release and security bulletins on the vendor support site. Confirm firmware signature verification / whitelisting is on (e.g. HP Code Signing / Sure Start, Xerox firmware verification, 'Allow firmware upgrade via PJL/print job' disabled) and that remote firmware upgrade is restricted to administrators.

remediation.command: Download the current firmware from the vendor support portal, verify its checksum/signature, and install via EWS (Firmware Upgrade) or fleet tooling during a maintenance window. Disable firmware upgrade via print jobs (PJL/port 9100) and enable signed-firmware enforcement.

title: Ensure the Embedded Web Server is accessible over HTTPS only with modern TLS
description: Admin credentials and device configuration are exchanged with the EWS; plain HTTP exposes them on the network. Use a trusted certificate, TLS 1.2+ and redirect or disable HTTP.
reference: CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 - Encrypt management traffic (HTTPS) (verify section number for your release)

audit.command: In the Embedded Web Server (EWS: browse to https://<printer-ip>/ and sign in as administrator; HP: Security / Networking tabs, Xerox: Properties > Security / Connectivity, Ricoh: Device Management > Configuration, Canon: Settings/Registration > Network Settings / Security Settings) > Security / Networking > Mgmt. Protocols or SSL/TLS settings: 'Encrypt all web communication' / 'Force HTTPS redirect' ON (http://<printer-ip>/ must redirect to https or be refused); TLS 1.0/1.1 and SSL 3.0 disabled, only TLS 1.2/1.3 with strong ciphers; the device certificate is issued by the organisation CA (not the factory self-signed one) and not expired. IPP should be IPPS (port 443/631 TLS) where clients support it.

remediation.command: EWS: install a CA-signed device certificate (Certificate Management), enable 'Encrypt all web communication' / HTTPS redirect, set minimum TLS version 1.2 and disable weak ciphers; disable plain HTTP and IPP where possible.

title: Ensure stored data is encrypted and securely erased (job overwrite and decommissioning)
description: Printer hard disks and flash keep copies of printed, scanned, copied and faxed documents. Storage encryption plus immediate image overwrite protects data at rest; a secure (cryptographic or DoD-style) erase is required before resale, return or disposal.
reference: CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 - Storage encryption and secure erase (verify section number for your release)

audit.command: In the Embedded Web Server (EWS: browse to https://<printer-ip>/ and sign in as administrator; HP: Security / Networking tabs, Xerox: Properties > Security / Connectivity, Ricoh: Device Management > Configuration, Canon: Settings/Registration > Network Settings / Security Settings) > Security > Stored Data Protection / Secure Storage (HP: Security > Protect Stored Data; Xerox: Security > Image Overwrite Security; Ricoh: Data Overwrite / Machine Data Encryption): storage encryption ON, 'Immediate Image Overwrite' / 'Secure Fast Erase' ON, and the decommissioning procedure (Secure Storage Erase / Sanitize, 'Erase All Data') is documented and evidenced for retired devices (certificate of sanitisation).

remediation.command: Enable the device's data encryption (Encrypted Hard Disk / Machine Data Encryption) and immediate image overwrite; before decommissioning run the vendor secure erase (e.g. HP 'Secure Sanitize Erase', Xerox 'On-Demand Image Overwrite - Full', Ricoh 'Erase All Memory') or destroy the drive, and record it.

title: Ensure SNMP is SNMPv3 only with authentication and privacy (or disabled)
description: SNMPv1/v2c community strings (public/private by default) are sent in clear text and often allow configuration writes, including resetting the admin password on some models. SNMPv3 authPriv protects management traffic.
reference: CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 - SNMP configuration (verify section number for your release)

audit.command: In the Embedded Web Server (EWS: browse to https://<printer-ip>/ and sign in as administrator; HP: Security / Networking tabs, Xerox: Properties > Security / Connectivity, Ricoh: Device Management > Configuration, Canon: Settings/Registration > Network Settings / Security Settings) > Networking > SNMP (Xerox: Connectivity > Setup > SNMP; Ricoh: Configuration > SNMPv3): SNMPv1/v2c disabled (or read-only with a non-default community if a monitoring tool cannot do v3), SNMPv3 enabled with security level authPriv using SHA (SHA-256 if available) and AES; no default 'public'/'private' community strings; write access restricted to the management station.

remediation.command: EWS: disable SNMPv1/v2c, enable SNMPv3, create a user with SHA authentication and AES privacy, update fleet management/monitoring tools to use SNMPv3 credentials.

title: Ensure unused and insecure network protocols are disabled (Telnet, FTP, SNMPv1/v2c, legacy print services)
description: Print devices enable many services by default. Telnet and FTP send credentials in clear text, SNMPv1/v2c use guessable community strings, and legacy services (LPD, raw 9100 with PJL file system access, WS-Discovery, AppleTalk/Bonjour, IPX, TFTP) widen the attack surface.
reference: CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 - Disable unused protocols and services (verify section number for your release)

audit.command: In the Embedded Web Server (EWS: browse to https://<printer-ip>/ and sign in as administrator; HP: Security / Networking tabs, Xerox: Properties > Security / Connectivity, Ricoh: Device Management > Configuration, Canon: Settings/Registration > Network Settings / Security Settings) > Networking / Network Settings > Protocols (HP: Networking > Other Settings / Mgmt. Protocols; Xerox: Connectivity > Setup): Telnet, FTP (printing and firmware), TFTP, SNMPv1/v2c, LPD, AppleTalk, IPX/SPX, WS-Discovery/WSD Print, SLP and other unused services must be OFF. Keep only the required print path (IPPS preferred). Confirm externally from an admin host with a port listing of the device (tcp/21, 23, 69, 515, 9100 closed unless justified; udp/161 v1/v2c rejected).

remediation.command: EWS: disable Telnet, FTP, TFTP, SNMPv1/v2c, LPD, WSD, SLP, AppleTalk/IPX and any unused print protocol; restrict raw port 9100 or disable PJL file system/device-control commands. Apply via fleet configuration templates.

title: Disable Serial Connectors
description: A serial port, such as RS232, is a physical interface, or connection, commonly used to connect computers, peripherals, and other consumer products. These interfaces are often used by legacy MFDs to provide administrative and diagnostic capabilities. It is recommended that serial connectors be disabled, where possible. Serial interfaces that expose administrative functionality may be abused by local attackers to compromise the MFD’s configuration and the data traversing it.

remediation.command: Follow the remediation procedure in CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 section 1.1.3 to configure: Disable Serial Connectors.

title: Require PIN for Administrative Control Panel
description: MFDs can commonly be configured to require an authorization code before granting access to the device’s control panel. It is recommended that authentication and authorization mechanisms be enabled for administrative control panel access. Requiring an authentication PIN to administer the MFD will ensure the availability of the device and the integrity and confidentiality of print, fax, and scan data.

title: Verify Configuration State after Power Loss
description: A defective Multi-Function Device may not retain its configuration state after power loss. It is recommended that the configuration state of the MDF be verified after power loss. If the configuration state of the MFD is not preserved in the absence of power, the device may be exposed to vulnerabilities manifest by its default configuration. 1.2 Hard Drive and Memory Protection This section provides guidance on securing hard disks and memory of a Multi-Function Device.

title: Utilize Chassis or Drive Lock
description: MFDs often come equipped with physical locks used to secure internal components. Utilizing a chassis or drive lock will aid in preventing the theft of internal components such as hard disks and memory. This will in turn protect the confidentiality and availability of print, fax, and scan data.
reference: CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 - 1.2.2 Utilize Chassis or Drive Lock

title: Delete Completed Scan Jobs
description: MFDs often have functionality that allows a user to scan an image to the MFD’s local hard drive. It is recommended that the MFD be configured to delete job artifacts once retrieved by the user. Ensuring that scanned images are deleted from the MFD will help ensure the confidentiality of sensitive data in the event a hard disk is stolen or discarded in an insecure manner.
reference: CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 - 1.2.3 Delete Completed Scan Jobs

title: Erase Hard Drive before Disposal or Return
description: MFDs often come equipped with an internal hard disk drive. By default, most manufacturers implement an image overwrite mechanism (also known as Immediate Image Overwrite) that overwrites temporary image files created during the print, network scan, scan-to-email, copy, and fax processes. Once the job has completed, the files are automatically overwritten. Typically, the system administrator can manually invoke this feature using the On Demand Image Overwrite (ODIO) function. Once invoked, ODIO cancels all copy, print, network scan, scan-to-email, and fax jobs, halts the printer interface, and overwrites the portions of the disk used for temporary data storage. It is recommended that this facility be used prior to returning, recycling, or otherwise disposing of the device. Ensuring that temporary files are overwritten will help ensure the confidentiality of sensitive data in the event...
reference: CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 - 1.2.4 Erase Hard Drive before Disposal or Return

remediation.command: Follow the remediation procedure in CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 section 1.2.4 to configure: Erase Hard Drive before Disposal or Return.

title: Establish Firmware Currency
description: The MFD’s operating logic that controls device functionality and service operation is often stored in firmware or Non-Volatile Random Access Memory (NVRAM). It is recommended that firmware revisions remain current. Ensuring firmware currency will eliminate exposure to published defects and vulnerabilities that have been mitigated in more recent firmware revisions. 2. Remote Device Management This section provides guidance on the secure configuration of the Remote Device Management features of Multi-Function Devices. 2.1 TCP/IP Configuration This section provides guidance on the secure configuration of the TCP/IP capabilities of Multi-Function Devices.

title: Set a Static IP Addresses
description: Network devices commonly support two distinct methods for obtaining an IP address; statically and dynamically. Statically assigned IP addresses are typically stored within the device’s NVRAM. Dynamically assigned IP addresses are typically obtained at device boot- time via one of many network-based broadcast mechanisms. It is recommended that a static IP address be assigned to the MFD. The use of static IP addresses reduces the device’s exposure to attacks against broadcast IP configuration mechanisms, such as DHCP and BOOTP. Additionally, static IP addresses may increase an organization’s ability to effectively monitor and protect the device from network-born threats as the device’s IP address will remain constant in Intrusion Detection System (IDS) logs and firewall policies.

title: Restrict Administrative Access to Specific IP Addresses
description: Many MFDs can be configured to limit administrative access to only those connections that originate from a designated IP subnet. It is recommended that access to network accessible administrative interfaces be limited to designated subnets. Restricting access to the MFD’s administrative interface to only a specific set of IP addresses will decrease exposure to unauthorized access. If the device lacks this functionality, use an access control list (ACL) in a router, firewall or switch to restrict access.

title: Disable Bootstrap Protocols
description: Bootstrap Protocols, including BOOTP, PXE, and DHCP are network protocols used by a network client to obtain its network configuration (IP, subnet, DNS servers, gateway, etc) automatically. It is recommended that bootstrap protocols be disabled. It has been previously recommended that MFD network configuration parameters be assigned statically. This configuration eliminates the need for the MFD to participate in the network bootstrapping process.

title: Disable Unused Protocols
description: Many MFDs can participate in networks that operate over a variety of protocols, including IP, IPX/SPX, and AppleTalk. As a defense in depth measure, it is recommended that all unused network-layer protocols supported by the MFD be disabled. This configuration will reduce risk introduced by vulnerabilities that are exposed over such protocols.

title: Disable Universal Plug and Play - UPnP
description: UPnP is designed to create a distributed plug-and-play environment over an IP network for the purpose of automatic device discovery, notification, and configuration. It is recommended that UPnP capabilities be disabled to reduce risk introduced by vulnerabilities that are exposed via this mechanism. If the UPnP capabilities of the MFD are mis-configured, a malicious entity may alter the MFD’s configuration which may lead to loss of data integrity, confidentiality, and/or availability.

title: Confirm Network Ports are Closed
description: Research has demonstrated that some MFDs suffer from a mismatch between the service state articulated in the management console and the true state of the service. Given this, it is recommended that the MFD undergo a port scan to ensure only expected network services are available. Performing a port scan on the MFD will validate that only expected network services are exposed. Additionally, results of the port scan will provide additional security assurance that the device is operating as expected or identify exposures that require additional attention.

remediation.command: Follow the remediation procedure in CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 section 2.1.7 to configure: Confirm Network Ports are Closed.

title: Limit Network Accessibility
description: Network devices, such as routers and firewalls can be configured to limit ingress traffic to the MFD. It is recommended that network traffic destined to the MFD be limited to authorized subnets and ports. Limiting the network accessibility of the MFD to only authorized subnets and ports will reduce the exposure of remotely accessible vulnerabilities affecting the MFD.

title: Restrict Print Services Ports
description: Print services are commonly bound to port 9100/TCP or 515/TCP. It is recommended that the MFD be configured to utilize these ports or a port standardized on by the implementing organization. Configuring the MFD to use a print service port that is known will help ensure the device is visible to network protection and monitoring solutions, such as intrusion detection systems and firewalls. 2.2 Wireless Access Configuration This section provides guidance on the secure configuration of the Wireless Access capabilities of Multi-Function Devices.

title: Disable Unused Wi-Fi Interfaces
description: MFDs often come equipped with Wi-Fi cards that allow these devices to participate on wireless LANs. As a defense in depth measure, it is recommended that unused Wi-Fi interfaces be disabled. This configuration will reduce risk introduced by vulnerabilities that are exposed over such interfaces. This configuration will also decrease exposure to flaws in the MFDs Wi-Fi protocol stacks.
reference: CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 - 2.2.2 Disable Unused Wi-Fi Interfaces

remediation.command: Follow the remediation procedure in CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 section 2.2.2 to configure: Disable Unused Wi-Fi Interfaces.

title: Disable RSH Access
description: RSH (remote shell) is a remote access service utilized by legacy MFDs. It is recommended that this access mechanism be disabled. The use of this protocol may create exposures to threats against the integrity of the MFD’s configuration, the confidentiality of authentication credentials used by the administrator, and the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data traversing the MFD. Given this, it is recommended that RSH services be disabled. The use of Secure Shell (SSH) is recommended in place of RSH. SSH mitigates the confidentiality and integrity threats that affect RSH.

remediation.command: Follow the remediation procedure in CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 section 2.3.1 to configure: Disable RSH Access.

title: Disable FTP Access
description: File Transfer Protocol (FTP) is a protocol designed to transfer files between networked devices. Often, MFDs allow users to upload print jobs and print files. Some MFDs also provide the ability to upload files (e.g. scanned documents) to a file server. It is recommended that this access mechanism be disabled. The use of this protocol may create exposures to threats against the integrity of the MFD’s configuration, the confidentiality of authentication credentials used by the administrator, and the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data traversing the MFD. Given this, it is recommended that FTP services be disabled. The use of FTP over SSH (SFTP) or FTP over TLS/SSL (FTPS) is recommended in place of FTP. SFTP and FTPS mitigate the confidentiality and integrity threats that affect FTP.

remediation.command: Follow the remediation procedure in CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 section 2.3.2 to configure: Disable FTP Access.

title: Disable Telnet Access
description: Telnet is a protocol designed to provide interactive text based shell access between networked devices. Legacy MFDs provide administrative access over this protocol. It is recommended that this access mechanism be disabled. The use of this protocol may create exposures to threats against the integrity of the MFD’s configuration, the confidentiality of authentication credentials used by the administrator, and the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data traversing the MFD. Given this, it is recommended that Telnet services be disabled. The use of Secure Shell (SSH) is recommended in place of Telnet. SSH mitigates the confidentiality and integrity threats that affect Telnet.

title: Secure SNMP Facilities
description: SNMP is a network management protocol used for centralized monitoring and configuration of network-based devices. SNMP "traps" are sent to a management console whenever an event occurs that warrants it (e.g. an "out-of-paper" or "paper jam" condition). The most basic form of SNMP security is the community string, which functions similarly to a password. Many devices come with preconfigured SNMP community strings which pose a security risk if left at the widely known, default settings - "public" for read-only access and "private" for read-write access. If SNMP is NOT used for device management in your environment, then disable it. If SNMP is used to monitor and/or manage the device, the following recommendations provide increasing levels of protection to better secure SNMP: 1. If only monitoring is necessary, disable SNMP read-write access. 2. Change the default SNMP community strings....

title: Disable Unused SMTP Services
description: Simple Mail Transport Protocol, (SMTP) is a protocol designed to transfer mail reliably and efficiently. Some MFDs accept inbound SMTP requests in support of SMTP-to-fax services. It is recommended that this access mechanism be disabled if unused. The use of this protocol may create exposures to threats against the confidentiality and integrity of print jobs. Given this, it is recommended that SMTP services be disabled. Additionally, it may be possible for a malicious entity to abuse MFD SMTP services for nefarious purposes, such as sending unsolicited email. SMTP over TLS/SSL will mitigate passive and casual attacks against the confidentiality and integrity of print jobs while in transit over SMTP. The use of SMTP over TLS is recommended in place of SMTP as it mitigates the confidentiality and integrity threats that affect SMTP.

title: Disable Unused HTTP Services
description: Hyper Text Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is the primary protocol over which web based communications occurs. Often, MFDs utilize this protocol to expose rich administrative interfaces. It is recommended that this access mechanism be disabled in favor of HTTPS. The use of this protocol may create exposures to threats against the integrity of the MFD’s configuration, the confidentiality of authentication credentials used by the administrator, and the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data traversing the MFD. Given this, it is recommended that HTTP services be disabled. The use of HTTP over TLS/SSL (HTTPS) is recommended in place of HTTP as HTTPS mitigates the confidentiality and integrity threats that affect HTTP.

Leveraging a job retrieval authorization mechanism, such as a PIN, will ensure the confidentiality of print, fax, and scan jobs.

title: Replace Self-Signed Certificates
description: Print devices often utilize self-signed certificates to protect the communication between administrators and management interfaces. This is most commonly found when managing the device via an HTTPS interface. It is recommended that self-signed certificates be replaced by certificates that chain to a trusted certificate authority. Self-signed certificates are less effective at ensuring that the communication between the administrator and the management interface is not victim to a man in the middle attack. This is because the identity of the certificate holder is not attested to by a trusted third party. Given this, it is more feasible for a malicious entity to compromise administrative communication by generating his/her own self-signed certificate and presenting that certificate to the administrator’s HTTPS client on behalf of the MFD. 7.2 File Shares

title: Ensure stored print jobs are PIN-protected and automatically deleted
description: Retained/stored jobs, scan-to-box documents and fax mailboxes can be reprinted or downloaded by anyone at the device or on the EWS. Require PIN/secure release and delete jobs automatically after a short period.
reference: CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 - Job storage and retention (verify section number for your release)

audit.command: In the Embedded Web Server (EWS: browse to https://<printer-ip>/ and sign in as administrator; HP: Security / Networking tabs, Xerox: Properties > Security / Connectivity, Ricoh: Device Management > Configuration, Canon: Settings/Registration > Network Settings / Security Settings) > Copy/Print > Job Storage (HP: Retrieve from Device Memory / Job Storage Settings; Xerox: Secure Print / Saved Jobs; Ricoh: Stored Documents / Locked Print): stored/private jobs require a PIN or authenticated pull-print release; 'Temporary job retention' / auto-delete of stored and secure jobs is set (e.g. 4 hours or less, held jobs deleted at power off); scan/fax mailboxes are password protected; job history on the EWS hides document names from non-admins.

remediation.command: EWS: enable secure (PIN) or authenticated pull print, set stored-job auto-delete to the shortest workable period, password-protect document boxes and fax mailboxes, and hide job names in job logs from non-administrators.

title: Ensure device security events are logged and forwarded to a central syslog/SIEM
description: Print devices keep only a small internal event log. Forwarding admin logins, configuration and firmware changes and failed authentications to syslog/SIEM lets compromise or misuse be detected and investigated.
reference: CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 - Logging and auditing (verify section number for your release)

audit.command: In the Embedded Web Server (EWS: browse to https://<printer-ip>/ and sign in as administrator; HP: Security / Networking tabs, Xerox: Properties > Security / Connectivity, Ricoh: Device Management > Configuration, Canon: Settings/Registration > Network Settings / Security Settings) > Security / Networking > Syslog or Audit Log (HP: Security > Syslog / Event Log; Xerox: Security > Audit Log; Ricoh: Device Management > Logs): audit logging ON, syslog server set to the central collector (TLS syslog where supported), severity covering security/authentication events; the device NTP/time server is configured so timestamps are correct; confirm in the SIEM that events from the device's IP were received recently.

remediation.command: EWS: enable the audit/security event log, configure the syslog destination (preferably TLS, tcp/6514), set NTP to the organisation time servers, and create a SIEM alert for admin logins, configuration changes and firmware updates.

title: Ensure management and print access is restricted to authorised networks
description: An IP access control list (or management VLAN) limits who can reach the EWS, SNMP and raw print ports, reducing exposure to network attacks and to accidental Internet exposure.
reference: CIS Multi-Function Device Benchmark v1.0.0 - Restrict network access to the device (verify section number for your release)

audit.command: In the Embedded Web Server (EWS: browse to https://<printer-ip>/ and sign in as administrator; HP: Security / Networking tabs, Xerox: Properties > Security / Connectivity, Ricoh: Device Management > Configuration, Canon: Settings/Registration > Network Settings / Security Settings) > Networking > Access Control List / IP Filter (Xerox: Connectivity > IP Filtering; Ricoh: Access Control): only the print server(s), management stations and user subnets are allowed, management (EWS/SNMP) limited to the admin subnet; the device is not reachable from the Internet (no NAT/port-forward, verify in external attack-surface scans); direct-to-device printing is limited if a print server is used.

remediation.command: EWS: configure the IP access control list / IP filter to allow only print servers and admin subnets for management; place printers in a dedicated VLAN with firewall rules; remove any Internet exposure.

title: Disable Firewire/1394 Connectors
description: Firewire is a physical interface, or connection, commonly used to connect computers, peripherals, and other consumer products. These interfaces are often used by MFDs to provide users with the ability to print documents stored on portable hard drives. It is recommended that Firewire ports be disabled. Firewire allows a device to have direct memory access (DMA), allowing it to perform I/O without the use of CPU resources. A device connected through a Firewire connection has the potential to write to and read from arbitrary memory locations in the MFD, potentially resulting in reduced levels of data integrity and confidentiality.

title: Disable Unused Bluetooth Interfaces
description: MFDs often provide administrators and users the ability to interact with the device via Bluetooth, a common short-range wireless communication protocol. Bluetooth allows a user to print and copy from their phone, PDA, or laptop. As a defense in depth measure, it is recommended that unused instances of this interface be disabled. Disabling Bluetooth interfaces will decrease exposure to latent vulnerabilities in the MFDs Bluetooth protocol parsing stack.
